newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian hospitals face new budget stringency.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian hospitals face new budget stringency.

text.p: Bulgaria's main university hospital said on Wednesday it was treating only emergency cases because of budget cuts caused by months of economic crisis and a new policy of austerity.
The Aleksandrovska Hospital, which has more than 1,200 beds, has suspended routine operations for three months from July 1.
"The situation is extremely difficult due to a lack of cash," the hospital's director, associate professor Dimitar Petkov, told Reuters.
"We are forced to suspend planned operations and will treat patients only from our region (a part of Sofia)," Petkov said.
Bulgaria pegged the lev to the mark on Tuesday under a so-called currency board system which requires that all levs in circulation be backed by foreign exchange reserves.

Under the austere 1997 budget, 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) is allocated to the health service, giving it 469 billion levs ($269 million). The original 1996 health budget was for the equivalent of $680.4 million.

The university hospital, where some 2,500 students study and practise each year, will get a total of 8.9 million levs from the health ministry for 1997, Petkov said, but it needs some 20 billion levs annually to operate normally.
"Our kidney transplant department has performed eight successful operations this year but I cannot allow risky operations now," Petkov said.
The hospital is forced to ask patients to supply their own bedsheets to save electricity, washing powder and staff at the laundry. Catering will be limited to sandwiches, rather than cooked meals.
Some patients will have to buy their medicines, although imported drugs are a major expense for state employees whose average monthly salary is some $83.
Sofia's Pirogov Hospital, Bulgaria's biggest emergency hospital, said it would curb non-essential medical tests for patients.
Pirogov's director, Professor Georgi Zlatarski, said the hospital expected to get some 800 million levs monthly from the health ministry, while it needed some $10-12 million per year.
He said Pirogov was the only hospital in the country which was not turning patients away. The hospital treats some 500,000 patients annually and hospitalises some 30,000 of them.
Pirogov receives emergency cases from the whole country but has only 1060 beds and often its corridors are packed with camp-beds.
"We will need more and more funds as the percentage of people injured in transport or criminal accidents is constantly rising," Zlatarski said.
The health ministry plans to audit hospitals to assess the quality of their services.

"The size of the subsidies to be extended will be based on these evaluations," said Deputy Health Minister Ilko Semerdjiev, who said the health ministry would cut ineffective health services in order to distribute funds where they were most needed.
